caseno: Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 8506 of 2002 and Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 8505 of 2002
lawyer:
Anisul Huque, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners in both the cases. 
Md Helal Uddin Mollah, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the State.
parties:
Nasim (Md) and another ------ Petitioners
vs 
State ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Sharif uddin Chaklader J: These two Rules, Rule of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 8505 of 2002 at the instance of AHS Rahman and Rule of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 8506 of 2002 at the instance of Md Nasim having arisen from same first information report, charge-sheet and of Special Case No. 73 of 2002 involving same facts, are taken up together for disposal and this judgment would govern both the Rules. 

 2. One Md Abdul Hai, Anti Corruption Officer, (Task force No.1) Anti Corruption Bureau, Bangladesh, Dhaka lodged the first information report on 8-1-2002 with the Ramna Police Station, relating to the occurrence between 22-11-98 and 12-7-2001 alleging that Md Nasim, at the relevant time, Post and Tele-Communication Minister and AHS Rahman, Director, Consociates Ltd in collusion with each other, by misusing their powers got Consociates Limited appointed as consultant of the project in a preplanned manner and without floating any further notice and without inviting any further international tender, gave the work of installing 3,00,000 telephone lines to World Tel Holding Ltd. It is the first information report case that Consociates Ltd recommended the proposal of World Tel Holding Ltd, is good enough for installing 3 lacs telephone lines. It has further been alleged there was no money sanctioned for appointing consultant but Md Nasim ordered to appoint consultant and arranged payment of fees of the consultant by World Tel Holding Ltd. Thereafter, the said consultant was entrusted to evaluate the financial proposal of only bidder, World Tel Holding as it was decided the World Tel Holding would pay the consultancy fees of Consociates Ltd, who opined the proposal of World Tel Holding as acceptable and without calling for further international tender, the agreement was signed with World Tel Holding. These facts constitute illegal connivance and also to facilitate World Tel Holding Ltd with the said job of installing 3 lacs digital telephones by which the Government has been in financial loss of huge amount and this act of these accused’s constituted offence under section 418/109 of the Penal Code and also offence punishable under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947. 

 3. In detail the first information report case is that on 22-11-1998 an international tender was called for installation of 3 lacs digital telephone lines and the said tender was participated by World Tel Holding Ltd, Bermuda, China Telecom Concepcion (joint venture of three companies) and Karnaphuli Ltd, Bangladesh (joint venture of HRC Bangladesh Ltd and Telecom Foundation of Pakistan) and to evaluate the quotation, Md Nasim, the then Minister held a meeting and by misusing his position, single handedly appointed Consociates Ltd as consultant, although there was no such provision. In that meeting, it was informed to the Minister that some other farms also applied for being appointed as a consultant but the Hon'ble Minister stick to his earlier decision of entrusting Consociates Ltd as consultant and by Memo dated 17-5-1999, this Consociates Ltd. was appointed as consultant. On 30-5-1999 a meeting was convened but the said meeting was not held as other members of the meeting, being engaged in different government works, could not attend. Thereafter, Consociates Ltd on 17-6-1999 opined the proposal of World Tel Holding Ltd as satisfactory and without taking into consideration of the financial proposal of the neighboring countries, opined the financial proposal of World Tel Holding Ltd as acceptable; in the meeting dated 21-7-1999, on the basis of the recommendation of the consultant, it was recommended for entering into agreement for licence with World Tel Holding Ltd., which was placed before the Cabinet meeting on 10-2-2000 and thereafter, on 12-7-2001 the Ministry of Post and Telegraph entered into an agreement with World Tel Holding Ltd. On enquiry, it was detected, although there was no fund for the consultant but the winning bidder, World Tel Ltd paid Taka 12,22,200 and $20,370 as per decision of Md Nasim to the consultant. These acts of the petitioners are punishable under section 418/109 of the Penal Code and under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947. 

 5. The accused petitioners appeared before the Court and they were enlarged on bail and thereafter they moved this Court on 17-8-2002. This date is very important for disposal of the Rule. At the time of issuance of the Rule, this Court stayed the proceeding of the aforesaid case, at first for a period 00 months, thereafter on 11-11-2002 the order of stay was extended till disposal of the Rule. 

 6. Mr Anisul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners of both the Rules, submits the occurrence disclosed in the first information report as well as charge-sheet, even on its face value, does not constitute the offence punishable under the sections mentioned in the charge-sheet. He further submits, petitioner ASH Rahman, was not in any way connected with affairs of the Ministry and gave his opinion as consultant, which was evaluated by several committees of the Ministry and also in the Cabinet meeting, as such, his opinion, if it was found unacceptable, the committee could have acted otherwise but the committee accepted his opinion, as such, he in no way, comes within the mischief of section 418 of the Penal Code, to the effect, under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947. The learned Advocate submitted that Md Nasim, being a public representative, might have committed wrong by giving order to appoint a consultant and also might have had a hand in appointing World Tel Holding Ltd for installing the required telephones in Dhaka City, but this wrong by itself is not an offence as public representative had to perform certain things, in which, he may not follow the norms and it might be irregular but it cannot be said to be an offence and it cannot be branded a penal offence punishable under any law of the country. Mr Huq further submits that the statements of the witnesses under section 161 of the Code does not disclose involvement of the accused petitioners in the impugned transaction and also does not disclose any dishonest intention or abuse of power of the petitioner. Mr Huq also submits the first information report does not disclose that the Government has suffered any loss by the actions of the petitioners. The learned Advocate further submits the entire allegations of first information report or charge-sheet do not constitute any offence under section 5(1) and 5(2) of Act II of 1947. Mr Anisul Huq also submits it is apparent from the records placed before the Court that at the end the prosecution on these materials will not be enable to bring home the charges levelled against the accused petitioners and no effective purpose will served in prolonging the litigation, which, in his opinion, is a harassment to the petitioners and at the same time, an abuse of the process of law and court. Learned Advocate further submits, petitioner AHS Rahman whatever he did was as a consultant and merely gave opinion which had no binding effect and it could have been refused or it may be accepted and in either case, he cannot be placed on trial as his such acts is neither falls within the ambit of section 418 of the Penal Code or section 5(2) of Act II, 1947. Mr Huq further submits that in the meeting of the Evaluation Committee dated 30-3-99 it 'was clearly stated that as the World Bank did not response to give financial assistance for payment of the fees of the consultant, the Ministry had decided that the winning bidder will bear the expenses of consultant. In support of his submission, learned Advocate relied on the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38. He also submits that the statements made under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, annexed as annexure C series, do not disclose any offence against the accused petitioners within the mischief of section 418 of the Penal Code and to that effect, under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947. He candidly submits, Md Nasim in no way can be said to be a public servant as he does not come within the defamation of public servant as per section 21 of the Penal Code. 

 8. Before considering the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner let us consider what are the condition which attracts section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, shortly the Code. It is no doubt an extraordinary power given to the High Court, which is called inherent jurisdiction of the High Court and since this power is extraordinary in nature and discretionary, it should be used sparingly, carefully and with utmost caution. Principally this extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court is attracted (i) to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the Code, (ii) to prevent abuse of the process of any Court and (iii) to secure ends of justice. To invoke this inherent jurisdiction of the court, the Code makes certain provisions and unless these provisions be exhausted, one cannot come to invoke section 561A of the Code to challenge .any proceeding or any order or judgment. The 3(three) conditions mentioned above, in general, call abashment proceeding. Code of Criminal Procedure enacted section 561A when the Code itself was codified in 1889. Thereafter, Code itself went through many changes. There were several amendments made in the Code and lastly, in Bangladesh, through Law Reform Ordinance of 1978 and Ordinance No. XXIV of 1982, the Code itself was modified and certain sections have been introduced. Law Reform Ordinance was given effect from 1-6-1979 and Ordinance No. XXIV of 1982 from 21-8-1982 and the sections which are made part of law now, are in aid of accused to challenge the proceeding. Unless these provisions which are now in CrPC be exhausted, the accused has no right to invoke section 561A of the Code. The laws are not brown papers to be avoided. It is made for implementation and to be followed. These provisions could be avoided if the accused, on the admitted fact, could make out a case of no evidence and only in that case, section 561 A of the Code could be invoked straight way. If the facts do not constitute any offence, the accused in that case, could invoke the provisions of section 241A, to that effect 265C of the Code for discharging him from prosecution and if the order goes against accused, he may move the Sessions Judge under section 439A of the Code or he may wait till framing of charge and could challenge the order framing charge before the Court of Sessions under section 439A of the Code. In the decision reported in 48 DLR 102, 50 DLR 301, 551 and 1995 BLD 188,226 it is settled unless the accused exhausted the provision of section 265C or 241 A of the Code, he/she has no right to invoke section 561A of the Code. But it may be borne in mind these two sections do not say the High Court Division looses it grip on section 561A of the Code 561A of the Code gives an extraordinary power only to High Court Division to pass any order to secure ends of justice 20 BLD (AD) 265 propounded the supremacy of section 561 A of the Code. Law Reform Ordinance, 1978 and Ordinance XXIV of 1982 gives accused an opportunity to come out of prosecution and since these laws paved the way to the accused for a favour before trial, the accused should avail this opportunity. These laws were enacted to relieve the High Court Division from the burden of frivolous use of section 561A of the Code. It is generally held unless the avenues be exhausted, one cannot invoke 561A of the Code. In spite of this legal position, if an accused finds the facts disclosed either in first information report or charge-sheet is so preposterous that no proceeding can be taken against him/her or the prosecution is legally barred in that case, the accused can straight way come to take shelter under section 561A of the Code without waiting for invoking section 261C or 241A of the Code. All these avenues are open to an accused before invoking the inherent jurisdiction of this Court. Section 561A of the Code is not a wishing cow to be milked at any time at the sweet will of the accused. 

 10. It is not denied the prosecution could be quashed even at the initial stage, as held by the Appellate Division of the Hon'able Supreme Court in the case of 28 DLR (AD) 38, when the court is of opinion the materials did not disclose any offence against the accused. On perusal of the first information report and charge-sheet we are of the view the instant case in no way falls within the aforesaid category. Mr Anisul Haque, the learned Advocate submits the materials do not disclose any offence either under section 418 of the Penal Code or section 5(2) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The learned Advocate submits anyone facing trial under section 418 of the Penal Code, the prosecution must show the offence comes within the definition of section 415 of the Penal Code. 

 12. On the submission of Mr Haq, we may refer to the decision reported in 14 DLR (SC) 235 wherein it has been held the word "person" has been defined in section 11 of the Code. It includes any Company or Association or body of persons, whether incorporated or not. Section 7 of the Code declares "every expression which is explained in any part of this Code, is used in every part of this Code in conformity with the explanation". This is in accordance with the general principle of construction of statutes that a term which occurs more than once in the same Act, must be given the same meaning throughout the Act, unless a special definition of the term or the requirement of a context leads to the contrary conclusion. Prima facie, therefore, the word "person" in section 415, Penal Code, should be held to cover "Government", unless some considerations inherent in the context of the section militate against that view. We find no such indication in the section itself, which could persuade us to cut down the connotation of "person" in this section to a "natural person" alone. It is significant the terms "man" and "woman" have also been defined in section 10 of the Code and if the legislature intended section 415 to be confined to a "natural person" alone, it could have placed the matter beyond all doubt by use of these terms rather than by the term "person". Section 27 of the Code lays down when property is in the possession of person's wife, clerk or servant, on account of the person, it is in that person's possession within the meaning of this Code. It would therefore, follow any Government property, in the possession of a Government servant, should be deemed to be in the possession of the Government, and if a person, by cheating a Government servant, induces either him or another Government servant, in consequence, to deliver to him certain property belonging to Government, there is no reason why the act of the person should not be held to be covered by section 415 of the Penal Code. In such a case, the "person" deceived would be the Government which could only act through one or other officer in its employment. So the submission made by the learned Advocate that the allegations in no way fulfill the requirement of law, in our view, is of no substance. 

 "Any public servant who commits or attempts to commit criminal misconduct shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 7 years or with fine or with both and pecuniary resources or property to which the criminal misconduct relates may also be confiscated to the state." 

 14. Criminal misconduct has been defined in section 5(1) of the said Act. To constitute an offence under this law, one of the ingredient is accused must be a public servant and he used corrupt or illegal means or otherwise abuse his official position as a public servant and he obtains for himself or for any other person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. Criminal Misconduct is of 7 categories mentioned in section 5(1)(a) to (e) and all these categories of misconduct have been made punishable under section 5(2) of the said Act and of the aforesaid categories of misconduct, section 5(1)(d) is relevant for this case, which is as follows "if he, by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant, obtain or attempts to obtain for himself or for any other person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage." 

 15. A public servant is said to be guilty of misconduct if he falls in either of the category mentioned in section 5(1) of Act II of 1947. It is to be seen when the accused by his own act or omission, made some illegal pecuniary benefits to him or to allow someone to act illegally or to facilitate someone by corrupt or illegal means, some benefits the accused squarely falls within the mischief of section 5(1) of the Act punishable under section 5(2) of the Act. The first information report disclosed involvement of accused petitioner, Md Nasim as he had a hand in getting the aforesaid work of installing 3 lacs digital telephone to World Tel Holding Ltd. Whether Md Nasim had a hand or not or whether he had mens rea or not, which is necessary ingredient of section 5(1) (d) of Act II of 1947 or whether Md Nasim directly involved or whether Md Nasim in appointing Rahman as a consultant or whether consultant Rahman was paid by World Tel Holding Ltd in absence of any fund of the Ministry for consultation fee or whether Md Nasim and Md Rahman benefited in giving the installation of said digital telephones to World Tel Holding Ltd and obtained undue benefit or otherwise abusing his possession as a public servant, all these queries are matter of trial and to be determined in trial after taking evidences. When evidence is required to determine the guilt or otherwise of the petitioner, the proceeding cannot be quashed. Our court in the decision reported in 19 DLR (SC) 369, 26 DLR (SC) 69, 31 DLR (SC) 69 and 32 DLR 182 deprecated abashment of proceeding immediately after submission of charge-sheet. 

 16. Mr Rahman, in his defence, took a ground that he as consultant, passed the opinion in favour of World Tel Holding Limited. However, it is the prosecution case World Tel Holding Ltd afterward getting the work order, paid him fee as consultant, when the Ministry of Telegraph and Telephone had no money for consultant's fee. This is enough to put him within the mischief of section 415, to the effect under section 418 of the Penal Code and also make him an abettor in the proceeding. Submission of Mr Anisul Haque, the learned Advocate that the offence disclosed does not attract any of the provision of section 415 to that effect 418 of the Penal Code and section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and the proceeding be quashed, is of no substance as the Court under section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is competent to alter or amend/modify the charge at any stage of the proceeding before pronouncement of judgment. 

 17. We have gone through the first information report to find out whether the allegations made therein is so preposterous that it does not constitute any offence against the accused petitioners. One of the branches of the argument of Mr Anisul Huq is that this first information report does not disclose any offence against either of the accused persons. We on a perusal of the same, find involvement of Md Nasim in appointing consultant without following rules of business, disclosed a fact, which is required to be established on trial. We also find the consultant so appointed, recommended for the company, which paid entire consultancy fees when there was no fund for the consultant. We do not know why the company would pay the consultancy fee. We find the first information report disclosed direct prima facie case against the accused petitioners. Moreover, this is a case where an officer, who is an inspector of Bureau of Anti- corruption lodged the first information report after examining several papers and documents lying with the Ministry. There is a distinction of lodging first information report by Bureau of Anti Corruption and by ordinary informant. Bureau of Anti-Corruption lodged first information report on examining papers finding the involvement of the accused therein and onus lies on the accused to explain his conduct. Just like wife's/husband's killing case wherein presence of the dead body in the premises of the accused is enough to link the accused with the murder unless the accused satisfactorily explain his/her conduct. Since the first information report has been filed on examining the papers and documents lying with the records of the Ministry, an onus automatically lies on the accused petitioners to explain in what circumstances and in what manner and in what form they acted in these matters, as such, we are of the opinion to prove or disprove the documents considered by the inspector of Bureau of Anti-corruption before lodging the first information report, needs a trial. 

 19. Much emphasis has been given by the learned Advocate Mr Anisul Huq on the decision of 28 DLR wherein it has been held a proceeding could be quashed even at the initial stage. This decision of 28 DLR (AD) 38 has been evaluated by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 87 wherein, Mr Justice ATM Afzal, as his Lordship was then, was of the opinion "there may be one case out of thousand cases where High Court Division will be justified in interference even at a initial stage before taking of cognizance." Law Reform Ordinance made certain provision for the accused for challenging prosecution. This Ordinance is in operation from 1-6-1979. 28 DLR (AD) 38 is of the year 1976. We have already observed by Law Reform Ordinance there is certain changes made in the Code importing certain provisions in aid of accused and we are of the opinion that before invoking section 561A of the Code the accused must exhaust the process of law now in existence. We find in the instant case charge-sheet was submitted on 13-6-2002 and the petitioner moved this court on 14-8-2002 without waiting for framing of charge or invoking the provisions of section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Since charge has not yet been framed, it is difficult on our part to stifle the proceeding at this initial stage. In the decision reported in 30 DLR (AD) 59, the Appellate Division disapproved quashing of the proceeding just immediately after submission of charge-sheet. From the facts disclosed in first information report and charge-sheet it cannot be said it is a case of no evidence against the accused petitioners. The accused petitioners in their petitions have alleged various facts and have given various arguments (22+ 19 grounds as taken in the Rule petitions) in their defence and tried to show they are innocent which, in our opinion, can be decided at the time of trial as the accused petitioners will have enough opportunity to establish their case for which section 561A of the Code is not the proper forum. 

 20. Mr Huq also submits statements of the witnesses under section 161 of the Code do not disclose any offence and do not attract involvement of the accused persons. Section 161 of the Code statements are merely statement used to contradict the witnesses on dock when they depose on oath. Section 161 of the Code statement is not a substantive piece of evidence. These statements have no evidentiary value. We are of the view the first information report and charge-sheet speak something which can be resolved or determined at trial. On a perusal of the first information report and charge-sheet we are of the view it cannot be said the instant proceeding is without any evidence. It is constant decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh that when on a reading of the first information report, charge-sheet and other materials, if it is of the opinion of the Court a prima facie case is disclosed, the case should not be quashed. If there is no evidence and prosecution failed to bring charge against the accused’s, they will be honourably acquitted. 

 21. It is not denied the police of the anticorruption department consider the alleged offences disclosed in the first information report to be a cognisable one and on completion of investigation, having found materials against accused petitioners, submitted charge-sheet whereupon the learned Magistrate having been satisfied about the prima facie case after submission of the charge-sheet by the police, issued warrant of arrest, in such circumstances it is difficult to say there were no materials to justify the charge-sheet. Since we are of the opinion this proceeding cannot be quashed at this stage, as we find the first information report and charge-sheet disclose a prima facie case against the accused petitioners and the prosecution is not legally barred, we find no substance in this Rule.
